aliases: time dilation between two clock events
purpose: How can the same pair of clock events have two elapsed-time readings?
meaning: For two events at the same position in the rest frame of an ideal inertial clock, its proper elapsed time is τ. A laboratory inertial frame in which that clock moves with speed v assigns coordinate interval t=γτ, where β=v/c and γ=1/√(1−β²). The two events generally occupy different laboratory positions. The factor γ is at least one, and equals one when relative speed is zero.

definition.setting: An ideal coasting spacecraft clock marks a start event and a finish event. Choose its proper elapsed time τ and its speed fraction β relative to a laboratory. Compare the clock interval with the laboratory coordinate interval for those same two events, using one fixed seconds ruler.

signature.β: Dimensionless relative speed v divided by the vacuum speed of light c
signature.γ: Lorentz factor multiplying the proper interval
signature.τ: Proper elapsed time between the two events, in seconds on their common clock
signature.t: Laboratory coordinate elapsed time between the same two events, in seconds
signature.v: Clock speed relative to the laboratory, in metres per second
signature.c: Exact SI speed of light in vacuum, 299792458 metres per second
signature.x: Laboratory spatial separation of the two clock events, in metres

conditions: Both frames are inertial in flat spacetime with no gravitational field. The speed fraction β is 0–0.95, and the clock proper interval τ is 1–10 seconds. The two events occur at one place in the clock rest frame; the laboratory interval concerns this same pair of events.
definition.domain_notes: This compares coordinate time with proper time, not delayed visual arrival of clock signals. Laboratory event positions generally differ when the clock moves. No acceleration, gravity, round trip, twin-paradox journey or claim about arbitrary event pairs is modeled. Both interval bars use one fixed 0–35 second scale. Values printed after square-root evaluation are approximate.

examples.title: A four-second spacecraft clock
examples.question: How can the same pair of clock events have two elapsed-time readings?
examples.setting: An ideal coasting spacecraft clock marks a start event and a finish event. Choose its proper elapsed time τ and its speed fraction β relative to a laboratory. Compare the clock interval with the laboratory coordinate interval for those same two events, using one fixed seconds ruler.
assumptions: Both frames are inertial in flat spacetime with no gravitational field. The speed fraction β is 0–0.95, and the clock proper interval τ is 1–10 seconds. The two events occur at one place in the clock rest frame; the laboratory interval concerns this same pair of events.

steps.reason: Choose the dimensionless speed ratio and proper interval in seconds.

For this inertial clock-event pair the spacetime interval gives c²τ²=c²t²−x². With x=vt, division by c² gives τ²=t²(1−β²). The future-directed positive interval therefore satisfies t=τ/√(1−β²)=γτ. This uses the special-relativistic interval as a physical premise, not a consequence of Euclidean geometry alone.
At β=0.6 the Lorentz factor is 1.25. The clock records four seconds and the laboratory assigns five seconds to the same events.
